title: Digital Skills for Information Use
text:
Welcome
This book accompanies the course Digital Skills for Information Use (Competencias digitales para el uso de la información, code 19408, 3 ECTS, first year, second term), part of the Bachelor’s degree Transversal Training programme (Formación Transversal) at Universidad Carlos III de Madrid. Its aim is to help you find, evaluate and use information reliably and ethically, including when it is produced by artificial intelligence.
The book follows the four blocks of the official syllabus: evaluating the credibility of digital information, searching for and organising information, using it ethically (including references and plagiarism) and generative artificial intelligence for content creation.
This is the English edition of the book. The Spanish edition has the same content.

title: Digital Skills for Information Use
text:
Course objectives
By the end of the course you should be able to:

Recognise information overload and disinformation, and use digital information critically.
Identify, select and evaluate information sources, including social media as a source of scientific information.
Design search strategies on general and specialised platforms, and organise what you find.
Use information ethically, respecting intellectual property and avoiding plagiarism.
Create and manage references with a citation style.
Understand how generative artificial intelligence works, what it is useful for, what its limits are and what ethics and regulation say about its use.

title: Unit 1. Introduction. Information sources
text:
1. Information, overload and false information
Accessing information has never been so easy, and knowing which information is reliable has never been so hard. Bawden & Robinson (2009) describe the “dark side” of information: information overload (more information than can be processed), the anxiety it causes and other paradoxical effects, such as feeling less informed the more information you receive.
When it comes to false information, it is useful to distinguish:



Type
What it is
Example




Misinformation
False, but shared without intending to deceive
Forwarding an ineffective home remedy believing it works


Disinformation
False and created or spread to deceive
A campaign with invented data to influence an election


Malinformation
True, but used to cause harm
Publishing someone’s real personal data



Pennycook & Rand (2021) show that many people share false information not so much because of ideological bias as because of inattention: they do not stop to think whether it is true before sharing it. A short pause improves judgement.

title: Unit 1. Introduction. Information sources
text:
2. Critical, reflective and proactive use
Metzger & Flanagin (2013) explain that, online, people do not assess credibility systematically but with mental shortcuts (heuristics): reputation (a well-known brand seems reliable), endorsement by others (many reviews or likes), consistency (what is repeated on several sites), expectancy violation (a sloppy design or errors make us suspicious) and persuasive intent (if it looks like they want to sell us something, we distrust it). These shortcuts are useful, but they can be exploited: a fake website can imitate a well-known brand and reviews can be bought.
Using information critically means replacing the shortcut with a check when it matters. For this, lateral reading works better than vertical reading: instead of analysing the page in depth (it may be designed to look reliable), you open other tabs to find out what others say about that source and that claim. This is what professional fact-checkers do.
The SIFT method, proposed by Mike Caulfield, sums up lateral reading in four steps:

Stop: before reading or sharing, ask yourself whether you know the source.
Investigate the source: who is behind it and what interests do they have?
Find better coverage: what do other reliable sources say about the same thing?
Trace claims: find the primary source of the claim, quote or image.







Figure 1: Vertical versus lateral reading. Lateral reading leaves the page to check the source and the claim in other sources.

title: Unit 1. Introduction. Information sources
text:
3. Identifying, selecting and evaluating sources
Sources are usually classified as primary (original information: a research article, a dataset, a law, an interview), secondary (they analyse or summarise primary sources: a review, a textbook, a news story about a study) and tertiary (they help you find the others: catalogues, databases, encyclopaedias).
To select them, the key question is what do I need: a definition, up-to-date data, the scientific evidence on a topic, the legislation in force. To evaluate them, a useful checklist is:



Criterion
Questions




Authorship
Who signs it? Do they know the subject? Is there a responsible organisation?


Purpose
Does it inform, give an opinion, sell, persuade?


Currency
When was it published or updated? Does the date matter for your topic?


Accuracy
Does it cite its sources? Can it be checked? Does it agree with other reliable sources?


Review
Has it passed peer review, professional editing or no check at all?









Figure 2: Types of sources. We often find a tertiary or secondary source first; the job is to get to the primary one.

section: 4. Social media as a source of scientific information
text:
4. Social media as a source of scientific information
Social media is increasingly used to spread and discuss science. Sugimoto et al. (2017) review how researchers use it and how these mentions are measured (altmetrics). For a student, social media can help you discover recent research and debates, but it is not the source: you need to get to the original article. Remember that:

A viral post about a study may exaggerate or misinterpret its results.
Social media mentions measure attention, not quality or truth.
Preprints (versions before peer review) spread widely on social media and may change or never be published.

title: Unit 1. Introduction. Information sources
section: 5. Disinformation and libraries: the IFLA infographic
text:
5. Disinformation and libraries: the IFLA infographic
In 2017 the International Federation of Library Associations and Institutions (IFLA) published the infographic How to Spot Fake News, adapted from a 2016 FactCheck.org article. It starts from one idea: critical thinking is a key skill of media and information literacy, and libraries should teach and defend it. IFLA offers it for download, printing, translation and sharing in libraries, communities and social media.








Step
What the infographic proposes
In practice




1. Consider the source
Investigate the website, its mission and its contact information
Who publishes it? Is there a real “About us” and contact?


2. Read beyond
A striking headline seeks attention: what is the whole story?
Read the whole text, not just the headline or thumbnail


3. Check the author
A quick search: are they credible? Are they real?
Look for their professional profile or ORCID


4. Supporting sources
Click the links and check that the information supports the story
Trace the claim back to the original study or document


5. Check the date
Reposting old news does not make it relevant to current events
Look at the date of publication and of the data


6. Is it a joke?
If it is too outlandish, it may be satire
Check whether the outlet is satirical


7. Check your biases
Your own beliefs can affect your judgement
Be more suspicious of what confirms what you already thought


8. Ask the experts
Ask a librarian or consult a fact-checking site
University libraries, fact-checkers such as Full Fact or Maldita.es



IFLA’s eight steps and SIFT’s four moves (worked example 1) complement each other: SIFT organises the process into four quick moves based on lateral reading, and IFLA breaks down what to check in each source. Step 7, checking your own biases, is perhaps the hardest: we tend to accept without checking whatever matches our ideas (confirmation bias).

text:
Worked examples






NoteExample 1 · A news story about a study: lateral reading with SIFT



A headline says: “Study proves that sleeping less than six hours doubles the risk of failing”. The SIFT method (Mike Caulfield) proposes four quick moves:






Figure 3: The four moves of the SIFT method for evaluating online information.




Stop: before sharing or believing it, ask yourself what you know about the source and how the headline makes you feel. A bold, emotional headline calls for more care.
Investigate the source: open another tab and find out who publishes the story (an outlet with a science desk, a commercial blog?). This is lateral reading: you evaluate a source by reading what others say about it, not what it says about itself.
Find better coverage: look for the topic in other reliable sources; if it is important, other outlets or agencies will have reported it.
Trace claims: find the original study (title, journal, DOI) and compare: is it an observational study? With how many people? Does it say “doubles” or “is associated with”?

Typical result: the original study found an association in a survey of students at one university; the headline turned it into a general causal relationship. The correct claim would be: “In a survey, students who slept less than six hours failed more subjects”.








NoteExample 2 · Is this journal reliable?



You receive an email inviting you to publish your bachelor’s thesis in an “international, indexed journal with review in 72 hours” for €150. Checks, in order:

Is it in recognised directories? If it is open access, look for it in DOAJ (Directory of Open Access Journals). Check its ISSN on the ISSN portal.
Where does it say it is indexed? “Indexed” means nothing unless it says where; check in the databases themselves (Scopus, Web of Science, Dialnet, Latindex).
Editorial board: do these people exist? Do they know they are on the board? Are they from the field?
Review: serious peer review is not done in 72 hours.
Checklist: the Think. Check. Submit. initiative sums up these questions.

Conclusion: the combination of an unsolicited invitation, promised speed, vague indexing and a fee suggests a predatory journal. Do not send your work.








NoteExample 3 · A viral thread about a preprint



A thread on social media announces a “discovery” and links to medRxiv. What you need to know: a preprint is work that has not yet been peer reviewed. It can be valuable and fast, but it should be read with caution: check whether it has already been published in a journal (the preprint page usually links to it), whether other specialists have commented on it and whether the thread exaggerates the results. When you cite it, always say it is a preprint.

Basic. Classify these sources as primary, secondary or tertiary: an article presenting an experiment; an encyclopaedia; a systematic review.

See guidance
A good report cites verifiable evidence (a link to DOAJ or the database, editorial board names that have been checked, the published review and fee policy) and distinguishes between what has been checked and what could not be verified.

title: Unit 2. Information retrieval
section: 1. From the need to the strategy
text:
1. From the need to the strategy
Every search begins with an information need: what you want to know and why. Before typing anything into a search engine:

Formulate the question in one sentence: “How does mobile phone use affect university students’ academic performance?”.
Identify the concepts: mobile phone use, academic performance, university students.
Find synonyms and related terms for each concept, in English and, if useful, in other languages (smartphone, mobile phone, cell phone; academic performance, achievement; university students, undergraduates).
Decide the limits: language, dates, type of document.

Bates (1989) showed that real searching is not a single query that returns the perfect set, but a process she called berrypicking: the need changes as you read, you pick up useful pieces at each step and you use a variety of techniques (following an article’s references, searching for an author, browsing a journal). Marchionini (2006) calls exploratory search the kind that is used to learn about a topic, as opposed to looking up a single fact.

Each platform has its own syntax; each search engine’s help pages explain it. In addition, many databases use a controlled vocabulary (thesauri, subject headings): standardised terms that group synonyms and improve results.

title: Unit 2. Information retrieval
text:
3. Precision and recall
Two classic measures describe a search:

Precision: of what I have found, what proportion is useful?
Recall: of everything that would be useful, what proportion have I found?

They usually move in opposite directions: adding synonyms with OR increases recall and lowers precision; adding concepts with AND increases precision and lowers recall. A class assignment needs precision above all; a literature review needs recall.






Figure 2: Precision and recall with the same documents. A narrow search retrieves few documents, almost all relevant; a broad one retrieves almost all of them, but with a lot of noise.

5. Organising information
Finding is half the job: the other half is not losing what you found. It helps to:

Save your search strategy (where, with which terms, when and how many results), so you can repeat it and explain it.
Use a reference manager (Unit 4) to save documents with their details.

R practice: Boolean operators from the inside
A search engine treats each term as the set of documents that contain it. In R, intersect() is AND, union() is OR and setdiff() is NOT:







Exercise 2.1
How many documents does (mobile OR smartphone) AND performance return?








The third concept is performance.


r <- intersect(union(mobile, smartphone), performance)
length(r)
Six documents: 1, 2, 8, 13, 4 and 16. Without the synonym smartphone you would only have found four: adding synonyms with OR increases recall.




Exercise 2.2
You have reviewed the six results and only four are useful. Calculate the precision of the search.







Precision is relevant divided by results.


relevant <- 4
results <- 6
relevant / results
0.67: two out of three results are useful.

NoteExample 1 · From the question to the search string



Question: how does mobile phone use affect university students’ academic performance?

Split the question into concepts: (a) mobile phone, (b) academic performance, (c) university students.
Gather synonyms and variants for each concept:








Concept
Terms




Mobile phone
smartphone*, “mobile phone”, ”cell phone”


Academic performance
“academic performance”, “academic achievement”, grades


University students
universit, “higher education”, “college student”




Combine with OR within each concept and with AND between concepts:

(smartphone* OR "mobile phone*" OR "cell phone*") AND ("academic performance" OR "academic achievement" OR grades) AND (universit* OR "higher education" OR "college student*")

Limit the fields if there is too much noise: search in title, abstract and keywords (in Scopus, TITLE-ABS-KEY(...)).
Document the database, the date, the exact search string and the number of results.









NoteExample 2 · Too many or too few results




12,000 results (low precision): restrict to title and abstract; add a concept with AND; filter by year, language or document type; use exact phrases in quotation marks.
8 results (low recall): add synonyms with OR; use truncation (educa* retrieves education, educational, educator…); remove the least essential concept; search more databases; check the references of relevant articles (“snowball” searching).









NoteExample 3 · The same search on three platforms






Platform
Strength
Watch out for




Dialnet
Literature in Spanish, journals and theses from Spanish universities
Less international coverage


Scopus / Web of Science
Selected international coverage, field searching, citations
Access through institutional subscription; less literature in Spanish


Google Scholar
Breadth, full text, free versions
Low precision, no reproducible search; limited operators (intitle:, quotation marks, -)



It is best to combine them: start in a specialised or multidisciplinary database and complete with Google Scholar to find the full text.

Advanced. Run your search string in two databases, note the results, review the first 20 in each and calculate what proportion is relevant (approximate precision). Propose an adjustment to improve it.

See guidance
Present a table with database, date, search string, number of results and relevant documents among the first 20. The adjustment must be justified: if precision is low, restrict fields or add concepts; if known key documents are missing, add synonyms.

1. Information ethics
Using information ethically means acknowledging other people’s work, respecting their rights and not deceiving the readers of your own work. At university, this commitment is called academic integrity: honesty, trust, fairness, respect and responsibility in study and research.
crumbs: 3  Unit 3. Ethical use of information and plagiarism

title: Unit 3. Ethical use of information and plagiarism
text:
2. Intellectual property
In Spain, the Intellectual Property Act (Royal Legislative Decree 1/1996) protects original creations (texts, images, music, software…) from the moment they are created, without needing to register them. It distinguishes:

Moral rights: recognition of authorship and integrity of the work. They cannot be waived.
Economic rights (exploitation rights): reproduction, distribution, public communication and transformation. As a general rule, they last for the author’s whole life and 70 years after their death; after that the work enters the public domain.

The right of quotation (art. 32) allows you to include fragments of other people’s works without asking permission when it is done as a quotation or for analysis, commentary or critical judgement, for teaching or research purposes, to the extent justified by that purpose, and stating the source and the author’s name.
Creative Commons licences allow authors to authorise certain uses in advance. They combine four conditions: BY (attribution, present in all of them), SA (share alike), NC (non-commercial) and ND (no derivatives). This book, for example, is licensed CC BY 4.0.






Figure 1: What each Creative Commons licence allows.

title: Unit 3. Ethical use of information and plagiarism
text:
3. What plagiarism is
Plagiarism is presenting someone else’s work, ideas or words as your own without acknowledging them. Pecorari & Petrić (2014) distinguish intentional plagiarism from the kind that comes from not knowing how to write with sources, especially when learning to write in another language or in a new academic genre. Both are plagiarism, but the second is prevented by learning.



Type
What it is




Verbatim copying
Copying text without quotation marks or citation


Patchwriting
Copying while changing a few words or their order, keeping the structure of the original


Uncited paraphrase
Rewording someone else’s ideas well, but without citing the source


Plagiarism of ideas
Using someone else’s argument, data or structure without acknowledging it


Self-plagiarism
Reusing your own work that has already been assessed or published without saying so


Work done by others
Submitting work commissioned from someone else or generated by an AI as if it were your own



In this course, plagiarism or copying in any activity means losing the mark for that activity.






Figure 2: From plagiarism to ethical use: what changes is not the words, but whether you acknowledge the source.

4. How to write with sources without plagiarising

Quotation: the exact words, in quotation marks, with the reference (and the page, if there is one). For sentences that matter because of their exact wording.
Paraphrase: the author’s idea in your own words and your own structure, with the reference. Tip: read, close the text, write what you have understood and then check that it is not too similar to the original.
Summary: the main ideas of a long text, more briefly, with the reference.
Your own ideas: they do not need a citation, but they must be clearly distinguished from other people’s.
Common knowledge (widely known, easily checked facts): no citation needed. When in doubt, cite.

Similarity-checking software compares fragments of consecutive words. A simple approach is to split texts into groups of three words (trigrams) and calculate what proportion they share (Jaccard similarity: shared / total distinct):

Worked examples






NoteExample 1 · Paraphrasing step by step



Original text (invented for this example): “Peer review, despite its limitations, remains the main quality-control mechanism of the scientific literature, although its effectiveness in detecting errors has been questioned by numerous studies” (Pérez, 2021, p. 14).






Figure 3: Five steps to paraphrase without plagiarising.




Read and understand the whole text; then close the original.
Write from memory the idea in your own words and structure: Although it is debated whether it catches errors well, evaluation by specialists continues to be the central tool for guaranteeing the quality of what is published in science (Pérez, 2021).
Compare with the original: have you changed the structure and vocabulary, not just a few synonyms? Do you keep the meaning?
Cite the source even though you have paraphrased.

Bad example (patchwriting): Peer review, in spite of its limits, continues to be the principal quality-control mechanism of the scientific literature. It changes two words and keeps the structure: it is plagiarism even if cited, because it is presented as your own wording.








NoteExample 2 · Reusing an image with a Creative Commons licence



You want to use in your work a photograph from Wikimedia Commons licensed CC BY-SA 4.0. Full attribution follows the TASL rule: Title, Author, Source, License:

“UC3M Library” by Ana López, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0 (link to the image and to the licence).

If you modify it (for example, crop it), say so (“cropped from the original”). With SA (share alike), if you publish a derivative work, it must carry the same licence. With NC (non-commercial) you cannot use it in a commercial context; with ND (no derivatives) you cannot modify it.








NoteExample 3 · Reusing your own work



You want to use in your master’s thesis three pages of a paper you submitted for another course. Presenting it as new without saying so is self-plagiarism. The right approach: check the course rules, cite your earlier work like any other source and rework the text, or ask the teaching staff for permission if you are extending previous work.

1. Why cite
Citing serves to acknowledge other people’s work, show what your statements are based on, allow readers to find the sources and distinguish your ideas from those of others. Academic work has two related elements:

title: Units 4 and 5. References
text:
4. Reference managers
A reference manager stores documents with their details, organises them, inserts citations into the word processor and generates the bibliography in any style. Gilmour & Cobus-Kuo (2011) compared several managers and found that they all make mistakes when generating references (capitalisation, missing data, name formats), so you must always check them. The most widely used are Zotero (free and open source), Mendeley and EndNote.
A recommended workflow:

Capture the reference from the database or the browser (with the manager’s connector).
Check and complete the details.
Organise them in collections and tags.
Cite from the word processor with the manager’s plug-in.
Review the final bibliography.

title: Units 4 and 5. References
text:
5. Similarity-checking tools
Universities use software that compares assignments with large text databases and flags overlaps. Foltýnek et al. (2020) evaluated many of these tools and concluded that they detect verbatim copying well but struggle with modifications (paraphrase, synonyms, translations), and that none is perfect. The similarity report is an indication, not a verdict: a well-made quotation matches its source and is not plagiarism, and an uncited paraphrase may not match and still be plagiarism.

title: Units 6 and 7. Generative artificial intelligence: foundations and applications
text:
1. What generative AI is
Generative artificial intelligence produces new content (text, images, audio, code) from patterns learned from large amounts of data. Conversational assistants are based on language models: systems trained on huge collections of texts to predict the most likely word (in fact, word fragment) that follows a given text. By repeating that prediction again and again, the model writes fluent answers.
Three important consequences follow:

The model produces what is plausible, not necessarily what is true. Bender et al. (2021) critically called them “stochastic parrots”: they combine linguistic forms without their own access to meaning or facts.
What it knows depends on its training data: it may not know recent facts and may reproduce the biases in those data.
How you ask matters: a clear prompt, with context, goal and format, gives better results.







Figure 1: How a language model generates text: it estimates the probability of each possible continuation and chooses one; then it repeats. Nothing in the process checks that the result is true.



Some systems combine the model with a search engine or a document collection and answer from what they retrieve (retrieval-augmented generation). This improves currency and makes it possible to link sources, but it does not eliminate errors: you must check that the source says what the system claims.
crumbs: 5  Units 6 and 7. Generative artificial intelligence: foundations and applications

title: Units 6 and 7. Generative artificial intelligence: foundations and applications
text:
2. Innovative applications and technical challenges
Generative AI is already used to draft and translate texts, summarise documents, write and review code, create images, audio and video, support customer service with conversational assistants and help search for and organise information. In information and documentation, applications include automatic description of collections, transcription of historical documents and search engines that answer in natural language citing their sources.
Its technical challenges define the open lines of research:







Challenge
What it involves




Truthfulness
Reducing hallucinations and grounding answers in verifiable sources


Currency
Incorporating information after training without retraining the whole model


Explainability
Understanding why the model produces a particular answer


Bias
Detecting and mitigating biases inherited from the data


Efficiency
Reducing the energy consumption and cost of training and using the models


Evaluation
Reliably measuring what they can do and where they fail


Detection
Distinguishing generated content from human content, which cannot be done reliably today

title: Units 6 and 7. Generative artificial intelligence: foundations and applications
text:
3. Hallucinations
A hallucination is an answer that looks correct but is false or invented. In academic work, the most dangerous one is the fabricated reference: an article with plausible authors, title, journal and DOI that does not exist. Walters & Wilder (2023) asked ChatGPT for short literature reviews and checked every reference: a large share of GPT-3.5’s citations were fabricated, and with GPT-4 a smaller but noticeable proportion remained; in addition, many real references contained errors.






Figure 2: How a fabricated reference arises. The model combines plausible pieces (a real author, a real journal, a title on the topic) into a reference that does not exist; only checking in a database reveals it.

Worked examples






NoteExample 1 · Auditing a bibliography generated by an AI



You ask an assistant for five references on “reproducibility in psychology”. Procedure for each reference:

Does it have a DOI? Open it at https://doi.org/ followed by the DOI. If it does not resolve, be suspicious.
If it resolves, compare title, authors, journal and year with what the AI gave: sometimes the DOI exists but belongs to another article.
If it has no DOI, search for the exact title in quotation marks in Google Scholar, Crossref or OpenAlex.
Classify each reference: correct, with errors (year, authors, pages) or fabricated.
Do not use any reference you have not located and read at least in its abstract.

Common result: some references are real, others mix the authors of one work with the title of another, and one does not exist. This is what is known as a hallucination: the model generates plausible text, it does not query a database (unless it uses a search tool, and even then it is worth checking).








NoteExample 2 · Improving a prompt



Vague prompt: “Tell me about open science”.
Improved prompt: > Act as a tutor for an undergraduate student of Information Science. Explain in 300 words what open science is, with three examples of practices (open access, open data, preregistration). Use clear language. Do not include references: I will search for them myself in databases. At the end, suggest three questions to check whether I have understood.
Elements that improve the result: role, audience, specific task, length, format and limits (here, avoiding references that could be fabricated).








NoteExample 3 · A figure that sounds right



An AI states: “70% of psychology studies cannot be replicated, according to the 2015 project”. Verification: the Open Science Collaboration (2015) project replicated 100 studies and obtained significant results in the same direction in 36% of the replications, compared with 97% of the originals. The AI’s figure is a simplification that mixes criteria: you need to go to the source and cite the exact figure with its definition.

1. Ethical principles of AI
Floridi & Cowls (2019) compared the main international statements on AI ethics and summarised them in five principles:



Principle
What it means




Beneficence
Promoting the well-being of people and the planet


Non-maleficence
Avoiding harm: privacy, security, misuse


Autonomy
People keep the power to decide


Justice
Sharing benefits, avoiding discrimination


Explicability
Being able to understand how it works and who is accountable



The first four come from bioethics; the fifth is specific to AI and makes the others possible.

title: Units 8 and 9. Generative artificial intelligence: ethics, authorship and regulation
text:
2. Ethical risks in everyday use

Bias: models reproduce the biases in their training data (gender, origin, language). An answer can look neutral and be biased underneath.
Consent, privacy and informational self-determination: informational self-determination is each person’s right to decide what is done with their personal data; in Spain, the Constitutional Court recognises it as the fundamental right to data protection. Models are often trained on data collected from the internet without their authors’ consent, and what you write into an assistant may be stored and, depending on the service, used to train models. Do not enter your own or other people’s personal data, or confidential documents, and check the service’s privacy settings.
Authorship and intellectual property: a generated text is not yours; moreover, models are trained on protected works, an open legal debate.
Dependence and learning: delegating to AI what the course wants you to learn prevents you from learning it.
Environmental cost: training and using large models consumes a lot of energy and water (Bender, Gebru, et al., 2021).

title: Units 8 and 9. Generative artificial intelligence: ethics, authorship and regulation
text:
3. Responsibility, authorship and transparency
In academic work, the general rule is transparency: if you use AI, say so, explain what for and take responsibility for the result. Scientific publishers and COPE (Committee on Publication Ethics) agree that an AI cannot be an author, because it cannot take responsibility for the work.
A useful statement says which tool (and version), what for it was used, in which parts and how the result was checked. For example:

AI use statement: I used [tool, version] to check the spelling and clarity of sections 2 and 3, and to suggest synonyms in the table of search terms. I reviewed and accepted or rejected each suggestion. The searches, the selection of documents and the conclusions are my own. I did not enter any personal data.

If the AI influences the content, APA also recommends citing it in the text and in the references, giving the prompt used in an appendix or in the text.






Figure 1: From use to statement: which tool, what for, in which parts and how it was checked.

4. The European regulatory framework
Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 on Artificial Intelligence (AI Act) is the first comprehensive law on AI. It follows a risk-based approach:








Risk level
Examples
Consequence




Unacceptable
Social scoring, manipulation causing harm
Prohibited


High
AI in education to assess or admit students, in employment, in essential services
Strict requirements: risk management, quality data, human oversight


Transparency
Conversational assistants, generated content (deepfakes)
Informing people that they are interacting with an AI or that the content is artificial


Minimal
Spam filters, video games
No specific obligations









Figure 2: The four risk levels of the EU AI Act.



The regulation also covers general-purpose AI models (the ones behind assistants) and requires those who deploy AI systems to ensure that their staff have a sufficient level of AI literacy. Its obligations apply in stages from 2025. Other rules, such as the General Data Protection Regulation, continue to apply to AI.

NoteExample 1 · Writing an AI use statement



In your bachelor’s thesis you used an AI assistant to check spelling and to suggest an initial structure for the table of contents. A suitable statement:

During the preparation of this work, [name of the tool, version] was used to check the spelling and grammar of the text and to obtain an initial proposal for the structure of the table of contents, which was modified by the author. All content was written, reviewed and verified by the author, who takes responsibility for the work. AI was not used to generate results, analyses or references.

Key elements: which tool, for which tasks, what you did and responsibility. Always check your university’s and your course’s rules.








NoteExample 2 · Personal data in a chatbot



To analyse the open-ended answers of a survey, you plan to paste them into a commercial chatbot. They contain names and comments about the participants’ health. Problems: they are personal data, some of them in a special category (health), and the GDPR requires a legal basis, information to participants and guarantees about where and how the data are processed. Alternatives: anonymise first (remove names and identifiable information), use tools approved by the university with contractual guarantees or do the analysis locally. When in doubt, ask the data protection officer.

title: Appendix D — Guide for teaching staff
text:
Assessed challenges
Each chapter ends with a challenge with no hint, solution or automatic marking. Each student chooses their own topic, claim or case, which makes copying harder. Challenges 2 and 4 are linked: the documents found in the search strategy are then managed in Zotero. They are submitted with the entrega_reto.qmd template, which includes a common rubric: searching and selecting sources (25%), critical evaluation (25%), ethical use and citation (20%), argumentation (20%) and presentation (10%). The template produces an HTML file with the images embedded, so the submission is a single file; it can also be submitted in the format the teaching staff indicate. No knowledge of R is needed to use it.
Reference solutions and marking criteria for the challenges are not in the public repository.

title: Appendix D — Guide for teaching staff
text:
Self-assessment in Aula Global
Each chapter’s self-assessment questions are exported to Moodle XML (Question bank → Import → Moodle XML format): one file per chapter and one with the whole bank. Each question keeps its explanation as general feedback, and the bank can be used to prepare the final test and the resit.

title: Appendix D — Guide for teaching staff
text:
Interactive activities and labs
As well as the self-assessment, each chapter has activities with instant feedback (ordering, classifying and decision scenarios) and several labs: searching OpenAlex with Boolean operators, comparing texts like a similarity checker, turning a DOI into an APA reference, verifying the DOIs an AI gives you and playing with a miniature language model. Labs with live data query open APIs (OpenAlex, Crossref and doi.org) directly from the student’s browser; nothing is sent to the book’s server. In the PDF and EPUB, the activities appear in printed form, with their solution.
The activities are written in Markdown with the interactivos extension (see _extensions/interactivos/interactivos.lua), so they can be added or changed without programming.

title: Appendix D — Guide for teaching staff
text:
The role of R
The book uses as little R as possible: four chapters have a short fill-in-the-blanks exercise that shows how a tool works inside (Boolean operators, ordering references, detecting overlaps, verifying DOIs). The chapter Using R in this book is enough preparation. No challenge requires programming.

title: Appendix D — Guide for teaching staff
text:
Book features

Class slides: each chapter has slides with the objectives, figures, main tables, the reading, discussion questions and the challenge. They are in diapositivas/; press F for full screen and S to see the notes.
Student progress: each chapter shows the exercises solved and the questions answered correctly; the welcome page summarises them all. It is stored only in the student’s browser (localStorage): teaching staff cannot see it.
Offline use: a service worker (sw.js) stores the pages and the R engine after the first visit.
Light and dark mode, with accessibility audits (WCAG 2.1 AA) in both.
PDF and EPUB generated with python3 herramientas/pdf.py.

The .github/workflows/comprobar.yml workflow renders the book and checks all the exercises, questions and accessibility in light and dark mode in a real browser, and once a week it checks the external links. When you publish a new version, update version in CITATION.cff and run preparar.py again so that browsers refresh their copy.
The data in the exercises are invented for teaching purposes; there are no data on real people.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
Information sources
Terms in the book, ordered by chapter. Each entry links to the chapter where it is explained.

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
Information overload
A situation in which you receive more information than you can process, with effects such as anxiety or feeling less well informed. → Unit 1


Disinformation
False information created or spread with the intention to deceive. → Unit 1


Misinformation
False information shared without the intention to deceive. → Unit 1


Credibility
The degree to which a source or a message is perceived as trustworthy. Online it is often judged with mental shortcuts (heuristics) such as reputation or endorsement by others. → Unit 1


Lateral reading
A verification strategy that consists of leaving the page and consulting other sources about it and about what it claims, instead of analysing it only from the inside. → Unit 1


SIFT method
Mike Caulfield’s method for verifying information in four steps: stop, investigate the source, find better coverage and trace claims back to the original. → Unit 1


Primary source
A source containing original information: a research article, a dataset, a law or an interview. Secondary sources analyse or summarise it; tertiary sources help you find it. → Unit 1


Peer review
Evaluation of a piece of work by specialists in the field before it is published. → Unit 1


Altmetrics
Measurement of mentions of scientific publications on social media, in the news and in other online sources. It measures attention, not quality. → Unit 1

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
Information retrieval

Information need
What a person wants to know and why; it is the starting point of every search. → Unit 2


Boolean operator
A word that combines search terms as sets: AND requires all of them, OR accepts any of them and NOT excludes. → Unit 2


Truncation
The use of a symbol, usually the asterisk, to retrieve all the endings of a stem. → Unit 2


Field searching
A search limited to one part of the record, such as the title, the author or the abstract. → Unit 2


Precision
The proportion of retrieved results that are relevant. → Unit 2


Recall
The proportion of all relevant documents that the search retrieves. → Unit 2


Berrypicking
Marcia Bates’s model in which searching is a process that changes as you read, picking up useful information at each step. → Unit 2


Controlled vocabulary
A set of standardised terms (thesaurus, subject headings) that a database uses to describe documents and group synonyms. → Unit 2

title: Appendix E — Glossary
section: Ethical use of information and plagiarism
text:
Ethical use of information and plagiarism

Intellectual property
The set of authors’ rights over their original creations: moral rights (which cannot be waived) and economic rights. → Unit 3


Right of quotation
A limit to intellectual property that allows fragments of other people’s works to be included for analysis or commentary for teaching or research purposes, stating the source and the author. → Unit 3


Public domain
The status of a work whose economic rights have expired and which can be used freely, respecting moral rights. → Unit 3


Creative Commons licence
A licence with which the author authorises certain uses of their work in advance, combining the conditions BY, SA, NC and ND. → Unit 3


Plagiarism
Presenting someone else’s work, ideas or words as your own without acknowledging them. → Unit 3


Paraphrase
Expressing an author’s ideas in your own words and structure, accompanied by a citation. → Unit 3


Patchwriting
Copying a text while changing some words or their order, but keeping its structure. It is a form of plagiarism. → Unit 3


Academic integrity
A commitment to honesty, trust, fairness, respect and responsibility in study and research. → Unit 3

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
References

Citation
A short marker in the text that points to the source used, such as (Bates, 1989) or [3]. → Units 4 and 5


Reference
The full description of a source in the final list of a piece of work. → Units 4 and 5


Citation style
A set of rules establishing which details citations and references include, in what order and with what punctuation (APA, Vancouver, ISO 690…). → Units 4 and 5


Author-date system
A citation system that identifies the source in the text by surname and year, and orders the list alphabetically. → Units 4 and 5


Numeric system
A citation system that identifies the source with a number and orders the list by order of appearance. → Units 4 and 5


DOI
Digital Object Identifier. A permanent identifier for a digital document that resolves at https://doi.org/. → Units 4 and 5


Reference manager
Software that stores and organises references, inserts citations into the word processor and generates the bibliography in a style. → Units 4 and 5


Similarity-checking tool
Software that compares a text with large collections of documents and flags overlaps. Its report is an indication, not a verdict of plagiarism. → Units 4 and 5

title: Appendix E — Glossary
text:
Generative artificial intelligence

Generative artificial intelligence
AI that produces new content (text, images, audio, code) from patterns learned from large amounts of data. → Units 6 and 7


Language model
A system trained on large collections of texts to predict the most likely fragment that follows a given text. → Units 6 and 7


Prompt
The text with which you ask a generative AI system for something. → Units 6 and 7


Hallucination
An AI answer that looks correct but is false or invented, such as a non-existent reference. → Units 6 and 7


Training data
The collection of data with which a model is trained; it determines what the model knows and the biases it reproduces. → Units 6 and 7


Retrieval-augmented generation
RAG. A technique that combines a language model with a search engine or document collection to answer from what is retrieved. → Units 6 and 7


Algorithmic bias
A systematic error in an automated system that favours or disadvantages certain groups, often inherited from the data. → Units 8 and 9


AI use statement
A text stating which AI tool was used in a piece of work, what for, in which parts and how the result was checked. → Units 8 and 9


AI Act
Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, which regulates AI in the European Union with a risk-based approach. → Units 8 and 9


AI literacy
The knowledge and skills needed to use AI in an informed way and understand its opportunities, risks and possible harms. → Units 8 and 9


Explicability
An ethical principle according to which it must be possible to understand how an AI system works and who is accountable for it. → Units 8 and 9


Personal data
Any information about an identified or identifiable natural person. → Units 8 and 9


Informational self-determination
Each person’s right to decide on the use of their personal data. → Units 8 and 9
